items.stem: In a systems diagram, what do boxes usually represent?

items.stem: Outline why the systems approach is useful in environmental science.
items.answer: Environmental issues involve many interacting parts across ecological, social and economic components; a systems approach shows flows, storages and feedback, allows prediction, reveals unintended consequences and links disciplines.

items.stem: "A sealed terrarium is an isolated system." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It exchanges energy (light in, heat out), so it is a closed system; an isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy.
items.markingKey: It exchanges energy (light in, heat out), so it is a closed system; an isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Systems description - a tropical forest plot: storages: living biomass 300 t C/ha, soil 120 t C/ha, litter 5 t C/ha; flows: photosynthesis 25 t C/ha/yr, plant and soil respiration 24 t C/ha/yr, litterfall 8 t C/ha/yr, decomposition 8 t C/ha/yr.

Calculate the total carbon storage of the plot and the net annual exchange with the atmosphere.
items.answer: 300 + 120 + 5 = 425 t C/ha; net uptake = 25 − 24 = 1 t C/ha/yr (a small sink).
items.markingKey: 300 + 120 + 5 = 425 t C/ha; net uptake = 25 − 24 = 1 t C/ha/yr (a small sink). Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Biosphere 2, Arizona (1991-1993) shows the difficulty of maintaining a closed system.
items.answer: Eight people lived in a sealed 1.27 ha structure; oxygen fell from about 21% to 14% and oxygen had to be pumped in. Soil microbes respired more than expected and concrete absorbed CO₂, showing that matter cycling in closed systems is hard to balance.
items.markingKey: Context (Eight people lived in a sealed 1.27 ha structure; oxygen fell from about 21% to 14% and oxygen had to be pumped in.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Soil microbes respired more than expected and concrete absorbed CO₂, showing that matter cycling in closed systems is hard to balance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the difficulty of maintaining a closed system.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "A systems approach is more useful than a reductionist approach for understanding environmental issues."
items.answer: Both are needed: reductionist studies provide data, and the systems approach integrates them to understand whole issues.
items.markingKey: For: shows interactions and feedback. Against: reductionist experiments give precise cause-and-effect evidence. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Treating Earth as a closed system is a useful basis for environmental management."
items.answer: The closed-system model is a powerful reminder of finite matter and the need for circularity, even though energy inputs are effectively continuous.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: emphasises that matter is finite and must be recycled; highlights waste accumulation (plastics, CO₂). Limitations / counter-points: Earth receives continuous solar energy, so energy is not finite in the same way; small inputs of matter (meteorites) and the scale of the system make the analogy imperfect. Conclusion: The closed-system model is a powerful reminder of finite matter and the need for circularity, even though energy inputs are effectively continuous. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: Explain why boundaries of a system must be defined for a study.
items.answer: Defining a boundary decides which storages and flows are internal and which are inputs and outputs, allows measurement and comparison, and makes the scale of the study clear (e.g. a single field vs a watershed).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a flow and a storage.
items.answer: A storage is a stock of matter or energy held at a moment (e.g. carbon in soil, in tonnes); a flow is a rate of movement between storages or across the boundary (tonnes per year).
items.markingKey: A storage is a stock of matter or energy held at a moment (e.g. carbon in soil, in tonnes); a flow is a rate of movement between storages or across the boundary (tonnes per year). items.stem: A valley glacier in the Alps stores 387 million m³ water equivalent. Each year it receives 61 million m³ water equivalent from snowfall accumulation and loses 56 million m³ water equivalent through melting and sublimation. Calculate the change in storage after one year and state whether the system is in steady state.
items.answer: ΔS = inputs − outputs = 61 − 56 = +5 million m³ water equivalent; storage = 392 million m³ water equivalent; not in steady state (inputs ≠ outputs)
items.markingKey: M1 inputs − outputs; A1 +5 (storage 392).

items.stem: Outline one way in which snowshoe hare and Canada lynx populations shows negative feedback in predator-prey systems.
items.answer: Hudson's Bay Company fur records show roughly 10-year cycles in both species, with lynx peaks lagging hare peaks. More hares support more lynx, whose predation reduces hares, which then reduces lynx - the populations oscillate about an equilibrium.
items.markingKey: Context (Hudson's Bay Company fur records show roughly 10-year cycles in both species, with lynx peaks lagging hare peaks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using the Silver Springs ecosystem, Florida (H.T. Odum, 1957) as an example, explain the second law of thermodynamics in ecosystems.

(a) Identify one quantitative piece of evidence in the extract. (b) Use it to outline the difficulty of maintaining a closed system.
items.answer: (a) any figure quoted from the extract with its unit/context, e.g. "Eight people lived in a sealed 1.27 ha structure; oxygen fell from about 21% to 14% and oxygen had to be pumped in." (b) Soil microbes respired more than expected and concrete absorbed CO₂, showing that matter cycling in closed systems is hard to balance.
items.markingKey: Evidence quoted from the extract with figures/units [1]; Soil microbes respired more than expected and concrete absorbed CO₂, showing that matter cycling in closed systems is hard to balance. [1] per valid linked point up to [3].

items.stem: With reference to the Amazon rainforest, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in a potential tipping point driven by positive feedback. [7]
items.answer: About 17-20% of the Amazon has been deforested; forest recycles rainfall through evapotranspiration, so loss reduces rainfall. Deforestation reduces moisture recycling, causing drought and fire, which kills more forest and could shift parts of the system to degraded savanna. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

Deforestation reduces moisture recycling, causing drought and fire, which kills more forest and could shift parts of the system to degraded savanna. items.stem: With reference to IPCC climate models (AR6, 2021), explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in the use and limitations of models. [7]
items.answer: Models project about 1.4 °C to 4.4 °C of warming by 2100 depending on the emissions scenario (SSP1-1.9 to SSP5-8.5). Scenarios allow decision-makers to compare pathways, but the range reflects uncertainty about emissions, feedback and cloud processes. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: In a car with a petrol engine, 2,000 kJ of chemical energy in petrol produces 600 kJ of kinetic energy. (a) Calculate the efficiency and the energy dissipated. (b) Use the first and second laws of thermodynamics to explain these figures.
items.answer: (a) 30%; 1,400 kJ lost as heat from the engine and exhaust (b) first law: energy is conserved, so input = useful output + losses (2,000 = 600 + 1,400); second law: every transformation is inefficient and increases entropy, so some energy is always degraded to low-grade heat that cannot do further work.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 30%, A1 1,400 kJ. (b) R1 first law (conservation), R1 second law (degradation to heat / entropy).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that tipping points make the precautionary principle essential in environmental management. [9]
items.answer: Because tipping points are uncertain and potentially irreversible, precautionary action is justified, particularly for high-impact global systems.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: thresholds are uncertain and changes may be irreversible; costs of crossing (Amazon dieback) are enormous. Arguments challenging it: precaution can delay development; some systems are more resilient than feared. A supported conclusion might be: Because tipping points are uncertain and potentially irreversible, precautionary action is justified, particularly for high-impact global systems. items.stem: Discuss, from more than one environmental value system, the view that computer models are the most reliable way to predict future environmental change. [9]

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the laws of thermodynamics place absolute limits on economic growth. [9]
items.answer: Thermodynamics limits material throughput, but growth in value through efficiency and renewables is possible within those limits.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: all production requires energy transformations that dissipate heat; resource use increases entropy; recycling cannot be 100%. Arguments challenging it: the Sun supplies a vast energy input (~174 PW), so energy is not the binding limit; growth can occur in services and efficiency. A supported conclusion might be: Thermodynamics limits material throughput, but growth in value through efficiency and renewables is possible within those limits. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The movement of matter or energy into, out of or within a system, shown by arrows in a systems diagram"?
items.answer: flow
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of flow.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A feedback loop that counteracts change and tends to return a system to its original state, promoting stability"?
items.answer: negative feedback
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of negative feedback.

items.stem: Which is the best example of an energy-to-matter transformation?
items.answer: Photosynthesis
items.markingKey: D. Light energy is converted into chemical energy stored in glucose.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the first law of thermodynamics and the second law of thermodynamics.
items.answer: The first law says energy is conserved (total input = total output); the second law says that in every transformation some energy is degraded to unusable heat, so efficiency is always below 100% and entropy rises.
items.markingKey: The first law says energy is conserved (total input = total output); the second law says that in every transformation some energy is degraded to unusable heat, so efficiency is always below 100% and entropy rises. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Systems diagrams show only physical components." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Systems in ESS can include social and economic components, e.g. a food system includes farmers, markets and consumers.
items.markingKey: Systems in ESS can include social and economic components, e.g. a food system includes farmers, markets and consumers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline why tipping points are difficult to predict.
items.answer: Systems are complex with many interacting feedbacks, time lags and non-linear responses; thresholds may only be recognised after they are crossed; data are limited and conditions vary.
items.markingKey: Systems are complex with many interacting feedbacks, time lags and non-linear responses; thresholds may only be recognised after they are crossed; data are limited and conditions vary. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Explain why photosynthesis and respiration are both examples of transformations.
items.answer: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy and inorganic CO₂ and water into organic glucose; respiration transforms chemical energy into usable energy (ATP) and heat, and organic matter back to CO₂ and water.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy and inorganic CO₂ and water into organic glucose; respiration transforms chemical energy into usable energy (ATP) and heat, and organic matter back to CO₂ and water. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Energy is lost from ecosystems, so the first law of thermodynamics does not apply." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Energy is not destroyed; it leaves the ecosystem as heat. "Lost" means no longer available to organisms, consistent with the first law.
items.markingKey: Energy is not destroyed; it leaves the ecosystem as heat. "Lost" means no longer available to organisms, consistent with the first law. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a storage and a flow.
items.answer: A storage is a stock of matter or energy held at a moment (e.g. carbon in soil, in tonnes); a flow is a rate of movement between storages or across the boundary (tonnes per year).
items.markingKey: A storage is a stock of matter or energy held at a moment (e.g. carbon in soil, in tonnes); a flow is a rate of movement between storages or across the boundary (tonnes per year). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Graph description: Arctic September sea-ice extent (NSIDC) - 1980: 7.8 million km²; 2000: 6.3 million km²; 2012: 3.6 million km² (record low); 2020: 4.0 million km².

Calculate the percentage decrease in September sea-ice extent between 1980 and 2012.
items.markingKey: (7.8 − 3.6)/7.8 × 100 ≈ 54%. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: With reference to the Limits to Growth World3 model (1972), explain how it illustrates how models can influence debate.
items.answer: A computer model of population, resources, food and pollution projected overshoot and collapse in the 21st century under business as usual. It was criticised as too pessimistic but stimulated discussion of finite resources and sustainability.
items.markingKey: Context (A computer model of population, resources, food and pollution projected overshoot and collapse in the 21st century under business as usual.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It was criticised as too pessimistic but stimulated discussion of finite resources and sustainability. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how models can influence debate.

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (the Silver Springs ecosystem, Florida (H.T. Odum, 1957)): Producers fixed about 20,810 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ of GPP while top carnivores received only about 21 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.

Explain what this information reveals about the second law of thermodynamics in ecosystems.
items.answer: Energy declines by about two orders of magnitude at each step as respiration releases heat, so only about 0.1% of producer energy reaches top carnivores.

items.stem:
The resource booklet states: "Phosphorus inputs led to algal blooms in the 1960s-70s and again since 2011 (Toledo drinking water ban, 2014)." (source: Lake eutrophication in Lake Erie).

(a) Identify one quantitative piece of evidence in the extract. (b) Use it to outline a shift between alternative stable states.
items.answer: (a) any figure quoted from the extract with its unit/context, e.g. "Phosphorus inputs led to algal blooms in the 1960s-70s and again since 2011 (Toledo drinking water ban, 2014)." (b) Once phosphorus exceeds a threshold, the lake flips from clear water to algal dominance, and internal phosphorus release from sediments maintains the new state.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Description of a model of a sand-dune system: inputs - sand from the beach (wind transfer), seeds, solar energy; processes - colonisation by marram grass, accumulation of humus (transformation of dead organic matter); outputs - sand blown inland, heat.

Identify one transfer and one transformation in this model.
items.answer: Transfer: wind blowing sand from the beach; transformation: dead plant material decomposed into humus (or photosynthesis by marram).

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Treating Earth as a closed system is a useful basis for environmental management."
items.answer: The closed-system model is a powerful reminder of finite matter and the need for circularity, even though energy inputs are effectively continuous.
items.markingKey: For: emphasises that matter is finite and must be recycled. Against: Earth receives continuous solar energy, so energy is not finite in the same way. items.stem: "Human societies are more resilient than natural ecosystems." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]
items.answer: Human resilience depends on the resilience of the ecosystems that support it, so the two cannot be separated.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: technology, trade and planning allow adaptation; societies can learn and reorganise. Arguments challenging it: dependence on global supply chains creates vulnerability; societies depend on ecosystem services; past societies collapsed (Easter Island debate, Norse Greenland). A supported conclusion might be: Human resilience depends on the resilience of the ecosystems that support it, so the two cannot be separated. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that an understanding of the laws of thermodynamics should shape food and energy policy. [9]
items.answer: Thermodynamics provides a sound scientific basis for policies favouring efficiency and plant-rich diets, but must be balanced with social and economic realities.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: eating lower on the food chain saves ~90% of energy losses; energy efficiency reduces waste heat and fuel use. Arguments challenging it: cultural and economic factors dominate food choices; renewable energy makes efficiency less critical.
